title: Formed the Carnegie Steel Company by consolidating the Carnegie plants
statement: On July 1, 1892, Carnegie consolidated the Edgar Thomson, Homestead, and H. C. Frick & Company assets into the Carnegie Steel Company at Henry Clay Frick's proposal, creating the integrated operating entity that would dominate American steel for the next decade.
outcome: By 1899 the consolidated firm reported net profits of $21 million, the scale and profitability that made it J. P. Morgan's acquisition target in 1901.

title: Built the Edgar Thomson Steel Works as the first Bessemer rail mill
statement: In 1872 Carnegie began construction of the Edgar Thomson Steel Works at Braddock, Pennsylvania, named for Pennsylvania Railroad president J. Edgar Thomson, designing the plant around the Bessemer process he had seen in England and engaging Alexander Lyman Holley as the design engineer.
outcome: The works began producing Bessemer steel rails in September 1875 and returned an estimated 40% on the initial $100,000 investment, the seed capital for the Carnegie Steel system.

title: Locked out the Homestead workers during the 1892 strike
statement: On June 29, 1892, with Carnegie in Scotland, Henry Clay Frick as chairman locked out the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers after the existing wage scale expired, and on July 6 brought three hundred armed Pinkerton agents up the Monongahela, triggering a battle in which seven workers and three Pinkertons were killed.
outcome: The Pennsylvania militia arrived on July 12, the strike collapsed by November 20, the union was broken at Homestead for decades, and Carnegie's public image as the friend of labor was permanently damaged.

title: Sold Carnegie Steel to J. P. Morgan
statement: On March 2, 1901, Carnegie sold Carnegie Steel to J. P. Morgan in a deal arranged by Charles M. Schwab, accepting roughly $226 million in preferred stock and gold bonds for his personal share and refusing the common stock that would have given him another $100 million.
outcome: The transaction formed the United States Steel Corporation, capitalized at $1.4 billion and the world's first billion-dollar corporation, and provided Carnegie the corpus for his philanthropic phase.

title: Published the Gospel of Wealth essay
statement: In June 1889, Carnegie published the essay titled Wealth, later known as The Gospel of Wealth, in the North American Review, calling on the rich to use their surplus wealth for the general good over their lifetimes rather than bequeathing it to heirs.
outcome: The essay was republished in England in the Pall Mall Budget at Gladstone's request, drew formal replies from Cardinal Manning and other churchmen, and became the operating charter for Carnegie's philanthropic phase and the founding thesis of the Carnegie Corporation.

title: Founded the Carnegie Corporation of New York
statement: On June 9, 1911, Carnegie chartered the Carnegie Corporation of New York with an initial endowment of $125 million and the mission to promote the advancement and diffusion of knowledge and understanding, the capstone of his philanthropic architecture and the residual legatee of his personal fortune.
outcome: The Corporation has operated continuously for more than a century, funding the National Research Council, the Carnegie libraries, and the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, and remains one of the largest American private foundations.

title: Founded the Carnegie Technical Schools
statement: In 1900 Carnegie founded the Carnegie Technical Schools in Pittsburgh with an initial endowment of $1 million, originally stipulating that the school would not grant degrees and would train the sons and daughters of working-class families for practical industrial employment, with the motto My heart is in the work.
outcome: The institution was rechartered as the Carnegie Institute of Technology in 1912 and merged with the Mellon Institute in 1967 to form Carnegie Mellon University, today a leading American research university.

title: Established the Carnegie Hero Fund Commission
statement: On April 15, 1904, Carnegie established the Carnegie Hero Fund Commission in Pittsburgh with a $5 million trust fund, inspired by Selwyn M. Taylor and Daniel A. Lyle, who died in the rescue attempts after the Harwick Mine disaster on January 25, 1904.
outcome: The Fund has awarded more than 10,000 Carnegie Medals since 1904, has paid $40.5 million in grants, scholarships, and death benefits, and was expanded to ten European countries between 1908 and 1911, the institutional pattern Carnegie replicated for his other philanthropic programs.
